hypothesis: If domestic dogs descend from several distinct wild species, then genome-wide and mitochondrial variation of dog breeds will fall into two or more clades each sister to a different wild Canis/canid species (e.g. wolf, golden jackal, coyote), rather than all dogs forming a single clade nested within one wild species.
pass_criterion: In a phylogeny or D-statistic analysis of a panel of diverse dogs plus gray wolf, coyote, golden jackal, and other Canis outgroups, at least two well-supported dog clades (bootstrap or posterior at least 95%) have different wild species as their closest sister lineage, or at least 5% of the dog genome shows significant (Z above 3) excess allele sharing with a non-wolf Canis species that is not explained by post-domestication admixture.
fail_criterion: All dogs form a single monophyletic clade (bootstrap or posterior at least 95%) whose sister is gray wolf (Canis lupus), and no non-wolf Canis species shows significant excess allele sharing with dogs (D-statistic Z below 3, or introgression estimate below 1%).
interpretation: Darwin's "distinct wild species" is read as separate species-level lineages of Canis, such as wolf, jackal and coyote. His "descended from" is read as the ancestry of the domestic dog gene pool, not as later gene flow, so a modern reading must separate domestication ancestry from later introgression. His "geographical and other considerations" correspond to phylogeographic structure in genetic data. The test is deliberately strict: it asks for multiple species of origin, not the weaker claim of multiple wolf populations or multiple dog lineages. No dataset is assigned, because no single public dataset that I could verify is suitable.
no_dataset_reason: The test needs population-level whole-genome or mitogenome data for many dogs and several wild canids. The most obvious single NCBI resource, the dog reference assembly, is one genome and cannot decide the question. I tried to check the NCBI Datasets landing page for it, but the fetch was blocked by a browser-verification page, so I could not confirm it. I am not confident of the exact URL or DOI of any multi-sample resequencing dataset, such as published dog and wolf VCFs on Dryad or in the European Variation Archive. Under the no-fabrication rule I am returning null instead of guessing an identifier.
